healthcareSystem: Mixed public/private. Public hospitals provide basic care at low cost; private hospitals and clinics in Nairobi and Mombasa offer good quality care. Rural healthcare is very limited.
qualityNotes: Private hospitals in Nairobi and Mombasa offer good quality care comparable to regional standards. Public hospitals are overcrowded and under-resourced. Rural areas have very limited medical facilities — serious cases require evacuation to Nairobi or abroad. Pharmacies widely available in cities.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 8am-10pm; some 24-hour pharmacies in Nairobi and Mombasa; chains include Pharmácia Kenya, Nairobi Women's Hospital Pharmacy, and independent pharmacies
pharmacyTips: Many medications available OTC. Pharmacists are helpful. Bring a list of medications with generic names. Malaria prophylaxis is essential — bring your preferred brand as availability varies. In rural areas, pharmacy access is very limited — bring all medications you may need.
prescriptionRules: A prescription is required for prescription medications but enforcement varies. Antibiotics and many drugs available OTC. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare at customs.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Narcotics (morphine, tramadol, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Strong narcotics require strict documentation. Carry alternatives or minimal quantities with documentation.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Yellow fever certificate required for entry from endemic countries.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Required for visa on arrival / e-visa — must show proof of travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage.
travelInsurance.tips: Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is mandatory for entry and essential. Public hospitals have limited resources; serious cases require evacuation to Nairobi private hospitals or medical evacuation to South Africa or Europe ($10,000-50,000+). Ensure coverage includes safari activities, helicopter evacuation, and malaria treatment.

required: Yellow Fever (required for all travelers over 1 year of age; must have valid certificate)
recommended: Meningococcal meningitis (for travel during dry season, especially in the north)
Rabies (for animal exposure, especially dogs and wildlife)
Malaria prophylaxis (essential for most of Kenya)
vaccinations.notes: Yellow fever vaccination is required for ALL travelers entering Kenya — must present valid certificate. Malaria prophylaxis is strongly recommended for most of the country, especially during rainy seasons. Nairobi at altitude has lower malaria risk but prophylaxis is still recommended for travel to game parks.

waterNotes: Tap water is NOT safe to drink in Kenya. Use bottled or filtered water at all times. Avoid ice in drinks outside of hotels and reputable restaurants. Bottled water is cheap and widely available — use it exclusively for drinking and brushing teeth. Waterborne diseases are common.
foodSafetyTips: Be cautious with food from street vendors and small eateries. In hotels, lodges, and reputable restaurants, food is generally safe. Avoid raw salads and uncooked vegetables outside of upscale establishments. In safari lodges and coastal resorts, food standards are high. Stick to well-cooked foods served hot.
medicalTourismNote: Kenya is not a major medical tourism destination but Nairobi has good private hospitals that serve as a regional healthcare hub for East Africa. Some specialized procedures are available at lower costs than Western countries. For world-class medical tourism, Kenyans often travel to South Africa or India.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Kenya. Emergency numbers (999), yellow fever vaccination required, pharmacy tips, restricted medications, malaria precautions, and travel insurance advice.

hospitals.notes: Premier private hospital. International patient department.

dentalCare.availability: Dental care available in Nairobi. Limited in safari/rural areas.
dentalCare.costRange: KSh 2,000-5,000 ($15-38) for consultation; KSh 3,000-10,000 ($23-77) for fillings
dentalCare.notes: Nairobi has quality dental clinics. Bring dental supplies on safari.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: Aga Khan and Nairobi Hospital have dental departments.

mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Available in Nairobi. English is an official language.
mentalHealth.notes: Mental health services mainly in Nairobi. Limited outside the capital.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Kenya's accessibility is very limited outside modern hotels and hospitals.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Private hospitals in Nairobi are accessible. Rural facilities are not.
accessibilityInfo.transport: Limited accessible transport. Safari vehicles are not wheelchair adapted. Private drivers best option.
accessibilityInfo.tips: Safari lodges vary widely in accessibility — confirm before booking. Some lodges offer ground-floor rooms and adapted vehicles. Nairobi National Park has some accessible viewing points.

covidStatus.notes: Malaria, typhoid, and safari-related injuries are more relevant health concerns.

insuranceClaimProcess: Private hospitals require payment upfront or insurance guarantee. Flying Doctors (AMREF) provides medical evacuation from safari areas. Keep all receipts. Aga Khan provides English documentation.
